title: The Sale That Never Was
description: Was £49.99, now £18.99 — except it never cost £49.99. Case file #003 follows Larry (fictional) through Black Friday week: the store that stopped lying and lost $985 million, the mixer that was always on sale, the mattress-maker taken to court over its 'was' prices and countdown clocks — and three checks that catch a fake sale.

characters.larry: a cheerful middle-aged man with a round face and a thin moustache, wearing a loud yellow checked sports jacket and a red fedora

thumbnail.prompt: a large cream paper price tag with a red border hanging on the right side of the frame, its higher price struck through in red, plain cream background

sources: Which? (26 Nov 2024). Nine in 10 Black Friday deals cheaper or same price at other times of the year (227 deals, 8 retailers; Boots hair dryer £49.99/£18.99).
J.C. Penney Form 8-K, 27 Feb 2013 (fiscal 2012: net loss $985M; total sales −24.8%; comparable sales −25.2%).
Fortune (25 Jan 2012): 590 promotional events in 2011; Ron Johnson: "People are disgusted with the lack of integrity on pricing."
Los Angeles Times via CS Monitor (26 Jan 2012): 0.2% of revenue at full price; almost 73% at 50%+ off.
TIME (2013): $5 T-shirt re-tagged $6 before markdowns returned.
Consumer Reports (22 Jun 2013), 'Fake sales can cost you': KitchenAid mixer check (2012); Edgar Dworsky's 2003 Kohl's tracking (20 items, 103 days, 86%).
Checkbook (2018), via 6abc: 19 retailers; sale price usually the routine price.
Hinojos v. Kohl's Corp., 9th Cir. (21 May 2013).
City of Los Angeles complaints (8 Dec 2016); Daily Journal (8 Oct 2021): case against Kohl's and Macy's dismissed.
Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, Science. Ariely, Loewenstein & Prelec (2003), QJE. Fudenberg, Levine & Maniadis (2012), AEJ: Micro.
Ngwe (2018), Fake Discounts Drive Real Revenues in Retail — HBS Working Knowledge summary.
FTC Bureau of Economics (1992), An Analysis of Department Store Reference Pricing in Metropolitan Washington, D.C.
CMA v Emma Matratzen GmbH & Ors [2026] EWHC 1995 (Ch), 30 July 2026; consent order 22 May 2026.
FTC Guides Against Deceptive Pricing, 16 CFR 233.1 (1964). California Business & Professions Code §17501. EU Directive 2019/2161, Art. 6a.
Larry is a fictional character. Scenes marked 'Illustration' are illustrations.

beats.text: A hair dryer at Boots. Was forty-nine ninety-nine.

visual.prompt: a chrome 1950s hand-held hair dryer standing on a shop shelf beside a large blank cream paper price tag with a red border on a string, plain cream background, product shot

beats.text: Now eighteen ninety-nine.
In the twelve months before, it had never cost forty-nine ninety-nine there. Not once.

doc.headline: The £49.99 that wasn't
doc.body: A hair dryer was £18.99 on Black Friday, marked down from £49.99. It had never been £49.99 at Boots in the preceding 12 months.

beats.text: Larry is made up. The forty-nine ninety-nine was too. Case file number three. The sale that never was.
Suspect number one. Name: the was price. Aliases: original, regular, compare at.

visual.prompt: a single cream paper price tag with a thick red border hanging on a string from a small nail, a bold black line struck through its upper half, plain light grey wall, nothing else in the picture, studio lighting

beats.text: Last seen: every Black Friday.
It never touches your money. It just tells you how much you're saving.

beats.text: First, the evidence. Britain's Which? checked two hundred and twenty-seven Black Friday deals.

beats.text: Nine in ten were the same price, or cheaper, at other times of the year.

beats.text: So how regular is regular? One consumer advocate tracked twenty Kohl's items for a hundred and three days.

beats.text: Years later, Checkbook magazine tracked nineteen big retailers. Most of the time, the sale price simply was the price.

beats.label: Checkbook 2018

beats.text: A federal appeals court summed it up in three words: price advertisements matter.

doc.headline: Fake 'original' prices
doc.body: "Misinformation about a product's 'normal' price is, therefore, significant to many consumers ... In sum, price advertisements matter."

beats.text: Los Angeles sued four department-store chains over fake original prices.

beats.text: Turns out, proving a price was never real is harder than faking one.
Why does a made-up number work? Psychologists once spun a rigged wheel that stopped on ten or sixty-five, then asked people to guess a percentage.

visual.prompt: a 1950s fairground wheel of fortune in a psychology lab, a scientist in a white coat holding a clipboard beside it

beats.label: Experiment · 1974

beats.text: The sixty-five group guessed almost twice as high.
At MIT, students wrote down the last digits of their social security number, then bid on a keyboard.

visual.prompt: a 1950s university lecture room seen from the front, students with simple friendly cartoon faces writing numbers on small white cards, a cordless keyboard displayed on the lecturer's desk

beats.label: MIT · 2003

beats.text: High numbers bid fifty-six dollars. Low numbers, sixteen.
A later replication found the effect much weaker. Weaker, but not zero.

doc.headline: Replication 2012: effect much weaker
doc.body: Repeating the experiment, the authors found very weak anchoring effects on what people were willing to pay.

beats.text: And Harvard researchers found outlet shoppers paid about seventy-seven cents more for every extra dollar of original price.

beats.label: HBS · 2018

beats.text: If you like catching prices in the act, subscribe. The Inspector has more files.
In defence of the accused.
One: Penney tried honesty, and shoppers walked out. They wanted the hunt.

beats.text: Two: a sale can still be a deal. An FTC study checked twenty department-store regular prices.

visual.credit: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (no known restrictions)
visual.caption: Price tag drawing, 1942 · Library of Congress

beats.label: FTC study · 1992

beats.text: Twelve were higher than any rival charged. Yet the sale prices averaged about four percent below the competition.

doc.headline: Department store reference pricing
doc.body: In 12 of 20 items, the 'regular' price was above the highest competitor price. On average, sale prices were about 4% below competitor average prices.

beats.text: Three: nobody buys a mattress every month. Waiting for a sale is smart.

beats.text: The was price may be fiction. The saving isn't always. And the accomplice nobody arrests? Our love of a bargain.

beats.text: A fixed rule, the judge said, risked drawing the line in the wrong place.

beats.section: Friday 11:58 PM: The clock that resets
beats.text: The clock lost anyway. In May, Emma agreed its countdown timers must end when the sale really ends, and can't be reused on a similar deal within four weeks.

doc.source: CMA v Emma · consent order · 22 May 2026
doc.headline: Countdown timers
doc.body: Countdown timers must conclude at the same time as the sales promotion they apply to, and are not used on any substantially similar promotion within 28 days.
doc.highlight: conclude at the same time as the sales promotion

beats.section: Friday 11:58 PM: The clock that resets
beats.text: So what makes a was price real? America's rulebook says: a price you really offered, regularly, for a reasonably substantial time.

doc.source: FTC Guides Against Deceptive Pricing · 16 CFR 233.1 · 1964
doc.headline: Former price comparisons
doc.body: The former price must be the actual, bona fide price at which the article was offered to the public on a regular basis for a reasonably substantial period of time.
doc.highlight: offered to the public on a regular basis

beats.text: Its own example is a pen tagged ten dollars for a few days, just so seven-fifty can look like a bargain.

Three checks before you pay. One. Was it ever that price here? Look for a date.

beats.text: If the tag can't give you one, treat the was as decoration.

beats.text: Two. Check the price history. Free trackers show what a product really cost, week by week:
beats.label: Illustration

beats.text: Keepa or camelcamelcamel for Amazon in the US, PriceSpy or idealo in Britain and Europe.

beats.text: A was price that never shows up on the chart is a suspect.
Three. Find the floor. In the EU, the was price must be the thirty-day low. Everywhere else, search the exact model number.

visual.prompt: the shiny cream stand mixer seen from the side, a small blank metal model plate on its base, plain background

beats.text: Larry's mixer: ninety dollars cheaper, one click away.
Forget the percentage. Compare the price you'd pay with the price you could pay.
The sentence: a date on every tag, and a second look from you.
Larry closed his tab without buying the mixer. Then he checked the price again. Twice.
Case closed. The verdict. Guilty: the was price. Accomplice: the clock.
